Although the fraction $f(P)$ of informed voters is a function of the eventual majority choice $P$, such that more participants receive weaker signals, we examine whether there exists a Bayesian social welfare maximizing voting rule. Our results indicate that for certain preference profiles, no such rule exists, leading to an election crisis characterized by undefined majority status. Conversely, within specific regions of the parameter space, we propose a Bayesian rule and demonstrate its convergence to the correct option as poverty of knowledge among electors intensifies (under conditions of strong convexity, it is optimal; under milder convexity, it may exceed in utility other deterministic choices made based on partial profile information). In cases where a rule fails to exist, we further show that Bayesian randomization—utilizing the realized election result as a stochastic tiebreaker—yields a strictly higher expected number of well-off electors than any tie-prone deterministic option. Finally, this randomization strategy ensures that every informed individual can accurately deduce the true state by observing whether the election declares indecision.
